newsitem.title: USA: Fuhrman boasts were lies - newspaper cites report.
newsitem.headline: Fuhrman boasts were lies - newspaper cites report.

text.p: A report on a Los Angeles Police Department investigation concluded that ex-detective Mark Fuhrman, a key witness in the O.J. Simpson murder trial, lied when he boasted in a series of taped interviews about police misconduct, the Los Angeles Times said Friday.

But the report has angered the civilian Police Commission, which has ordered Police Chief Willie Williams and his staff to rewrite it, the newspaper said. It said the commission believed the LAPD analysis was poorly reasoned and incomplete and might complicate a continuing federal investigation of the police department.
Williams defended the investigation but conceded the commission was unhappy and told the Times he had ordered a new draft to be completed in the next few weeks.

Fuhrman, one of the first police officers at the scene of the June 12, 1994 murders of Simpson's ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman, pleaded no-contest this month to perjury in his testimony at the criminal trial.

After he denied on the stand using racial epithets in the last 10 years, a series of tape-recorded interviews with an aspiring screenwriter came to light in which Fuhrman was heard frequently using the word "nigger" and detailing police brutality and falsifying of evidence aginst blacks and other ethnic minorities.

Simpson's lawyers used the tapes to bolster their theory that the ex-football star was the victim of a police conspiracy. They labeled Fuhrman, who has since retired, a racist who planted a bloody glove on Simpson's property and accused the LAPD of bungling the investigation.
Simpson, who was acquitted of murder by a predominantly black jury at the criminal trial last year, has been sued in civil court by the families of the victims.

The Times, which said it obtained a copy of the executive summary of the LAPD investigation, said investigators had turned up incidents that paralleled those Fuhrman had told the screenwriter. But in almost every case, the inquiry concluded that Fuhrman was exaggerating or lying outright.

As a result, Williams and the LAPD leadership had decided not to sustain charges of brutality, racism and excessive use of force. The Times cited Police Commission members as saying they were concerned how it would be received by the U.S. Justice Department, which has requested a copy of the probe when it is completed.

Some commissioners fear the report does not candidly examine how an officer who demonstrated such apparent racism could be promoted through the ranks. As a result, they worry it might provoke federal authorities to step up their inquiry into LAPD operations, the newspaper reported.
